stem: A client has an indwelling epidural catheter for analgesia. Which insertion-site finding is most concerning for catheter-associated infection and requires prompt evaluation?

options.A: Redness, swelling, and purulent drainage at the catheter insertion site.
options.B: An intact dressing with no redness, swelling, or drainage.
options.C: Improved pain control with no new neurologic symptoms or site changes.
options.D: A secure catheter with the insertion site clean and dry.

rationale: ASRA notes that epidural or regional-block catheters can become infected and that the insertion site requires careful monitoring. Redness, swelling, and purulent discharge are signs that should prompt immediate inspection and catheter removal/evaluation. The other findings do not indicate insertion-site infection.
educational_objective: Recognize insertion-site findings that suggest infection in a client with an indwelling epidural catheter and require prompt action.
source_organization: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA Pain Medicine)
source_locator: Section 'Can the epidural or regional block catheter become infected?': careful monitoring of the insertion site; redness, swelling, and purulent discharge should prompt immediate inspection and removal of the catheter
source_claim_supported: Epidural/regional catheter insertion sites require monitoring for infection; redness, swelling, and purulent discharge are concerning findings requiring prompt inspection and catheter removal/evaluation.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p.13/PDF p.17: Monitor client for complications of diagnostic or therapeutic procedures; Recognize trends and changes in client condition
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — monitoring for epidural-catheter complications
correction_summary: Replaced the broad, weakly sourced bundle of epidural monitoring claims (pain relief, motor block, hypotension, respiratory depression, leakage, positioning) with a single directly sourced ASRA safety construct: insertion-site infection monitoring. Reclassified from Basic Care and Comfort to Reduction of Risk Potential because the item now tests recognition of a catheter complication.
